title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
keyIdea: Two equal halves exist only if some subset adds up to total / 2 (odd total → false). That is subset sum: for each number, take it or skip it. dp[index][sum] = can the numbers from index on bring sum to target; each row only needs the row below, so two rows are enough.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Take or skip each number, tracking the running sum; true when it hits target.
approaches.why: Two choices per number with nothing saved; the stack is n deep.

approaches.name: Memoization
approaches.idea: Same recursion; save the answer for each (index, sum) in dp so it is solved once.
approaches.why: n × (target + 1) states, O(1) work each; the dp table plus an n-deep stack.

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: dp[row][target] = true for every row; fill index from n − 1 up and sum from target down: dp[index][sum] = dp[index + 1][sum + arr[index]] || dp[index + 1][sum]. Answer dp[0][0].
approaches.why: Two nested loops over n indexes and target + 1 sums; the whole table is kept.

approaches.name: Tabulation, two rows
approaches.idea: Your active code: each row only reads the row below, so keep curr and next of size target + 1; after each index, next = curr. Answer next[0].
approaches.why: Same two loops; only two rows of target + 1 are stored.

quiz.q: Why look for a subset with sum = total / 2?
options: If one subset has half the total, the remaining numbers have the other half
It only works for even n

quiz.q: [1, 2, 3, 5]: why is the answer false immediately?
options: The total 11 is odd, so it can't split into two equal integer halves

quiz.q: Why can the table be reduced to two rows?
options: Row index only reads row index + 1

quiz.q: What does dp[index][target] equal, and why?
options: true: the sum already reached the target, nothing more is needed
